## Foundations {#foundations}

The building blocks you interact with directly, in every session.

::: {.term-entry}
### Claude Code

An agentic assistant that reads your files, edits them, runs commands, and
follows your instructions — available from a terminal, an IDE, a desktop
app, or a browser. It's what turns "describe what you want" into an actual
result, rather than just a chat reply.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Claude Code overview →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Memory

The system that lets Claude carry knowledge across sessions instead of
starting from zero every time. It has two parts: **CLAUDE.md** files you
write yourself — standing instructions at project, user, or organization
level — and **auto memory**, notes Claude writes to itself about
preferences and conventions it picks up as you work together. Both load
automatically as context at the start of a session; neither overrides the
other, but your explicit CLAUDE.md instructions take precedence when they
conflict.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Memory →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### CLAUDE.md

The most common piece of memory in practice: a markdown file in your project
that Claude reads automatically at the start of every session — your
standing instructions: brand, defaults, conventions, whatever you'd
otherwise have to re-explain in every chat.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Memory (CLAUDE.md) →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Skill

A saved, reusable set of instructions — written once in plain English — that
Claude can run again and again. You invoke one by typing `/` followed by its
name (a **slash command**). Skills follow Anthropic's open Agent Skills
standard — `/proposal-to-slides` is one example of a Skill in action.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Skills →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Slash command

How you run a Skill. Type `/` followed by the command's name — e.g.
`/proposal-to-slides` — and Claude executes the saved recipe. Claude Code
also ships built-in slash commands like `/model` (switch models), `/effort`
(switch reasoning effort), and `/memory` (manage CLAUDE.md).

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Slash commands →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands)
:::

[↑ Back to top](#top){.back-to-top}

:::

## Choosing a Model {#choosing-a-model}

Which "brain" does the work, and how hard it reasons before answering.

::: {.term-entry}
### Model

The actual AI doing the reasoning behind any Claude Code response. Claude
Code lets you pick which one runs a given task from a small picker in the
interface, trading off speed, cost, and depth of reasoning depending on what
you choose.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Models overview →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Claude Fable

Anthropic's most capable model overall — a tier above Opus, reserved for the
hardest reasoning and the longest, most autonomous agentic runs. Priced and
positioned above the everyday tiers, so reach for it only when a task
genuinely needs the extra depth, not as a default upgrade from Opus.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Models overview →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Claude Opus

Anthropic's most capable model in everyday use — for the hardest,
highest-stakes, or most open-ended work: a full rewrite, a tricky analysis,
anything you'd double-check carefully either way. Slower and more expensive
than Sonnet or Haiku.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Models overview →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Claude Sonnet

The best balance of speed and intelligence — near-Opus quality on most
writing, analysis, and Claude Code work. The sensible everyday default when
you're not sure which model to pick.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Models overview →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Claude Haiku

The fastest model, built for quick, well-defined tasks — proofreading, short
rewrites, simple formatting. Not built for deep reasoning, but the cheapest
and quickest option when a task doesn't need it.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Models overview →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview)
:::

## Working Within Limits {#working-within-limits}

The unit everything is measured in, and two dials that shape *how* a model
works on your task — worth knowing once a task gets hard or a conversation
runs long.

::: {.term-entry}
### Token

The basic unit Claude measures text in, for both what you send and what it
generates. Everything in a request counts toward token totals — the system
prompt, your messages, tool definitions, images and documents, and Claude's
own response, including any extended thinking. Token counts can also vary
by tokenizer version, so identical text doesn't always produce identical
counts across models; you can check the exact number for a request in
advance, or read it afterward from the response's usage data.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Token counting →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Context window

The total amount of text — your instructions, the conversation so far, file
contents — that Claude can hold onto and reference at once, measured in
tokens. As a conversation grows, older content can start crowding out what
matters, sometimes called *context rot*. Claude Code automatically compacts
long conversations to reclaim space, but you also have direct control: start
a fresh session for a new task instead of continuing an old one, run
`/clear` to reset deliberately, or delegate heavy exploration to a subagent
so it never touches your main conversation at all.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Context windows →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Effort level

Sometimes called *model effort* — the setting behind the "High" button on
the Claude Code screen, controlling how much the model reasons before
responding: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. Lower effort is
faster and cheaper for simple, well-defined tasks; higher effort gives the
model more room to reason through something genuinely hard. Change it
anytime with `/effort` or the model picker — no need to commit to one
setting for a whole session.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Model configuration →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config)
:::

[↑ Back to top](#top){.back-to-top}

:::

## Doing & Delegating {#doing-delegating}

How work actually gets executed once you've asked for something.

::: {.term-entry}
### Agent (subagent)

A specialized, independent Claude given its own task, its own tools, and its
own clean context window — separate from your main conversation. Because it
starts fresh, an agent isn't biased by what's already been discussed, which
is exactly why separating research from review across two agents produces
more reliable, less biased analysis. It also protects your main
conversation's context window from filling up with exploration you don't
need to keep around.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Subagents →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Tool use (tool calling)

The mechanism that lets Claude actually *do* things — call a function, run a
search, execute code — instead of only producing text. Claude decides when a
tool is needed and what to pass it; your application (or Claude Code itself)
runs it and returns the result.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Tool use →](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview)
:::

[↑ Back to top](#top){.back-to-top}

:::

::: {.thesaurus-category .cat-safety}

## Safety & Control {#safety-control}

The guardrails that keep Claude's actions visible and reversible.

::: {.term-entry}
### Sandbox

The safety boundary Claude operates inside. Risky actions — deleting files,
reaching the internet — are isolated at the operating-system level, so even
if something slips past a decision Claude makes, it can't reach beyond this
boundary. This is what lets you watch and say no, rather than discovering a
problem after the fact.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Sandboxing →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Permissions

The rule-based approval system that decides what Claude is actually allowed
to do — distinct from the Sandbox above. Read-only actions (reading a file,
searching the codebase) need no approval; anything that changes something
(running a command, editing a file) is checked against **allow**, **ask**,
or **deny** rules before it happens. Permissions and the Sandbox work
together as layered defenses: permissions stop Claude from *attempting* a
restricted action, and the Sandbox's OS-level isolation is the backstop if
something slips through anyway.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Permissions →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)
:::

::: {.term-entry}
### Hook

A command that runs automatically at a specific point in a Claude Code
session — for example, right before Claude uses a tool, or right when a
session starts. Hooks let you enforce policies or trigger integrations
without relying on Claude to remember to do it every time.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: Hooks →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)
:::

[↑ Back to top](#top){.back-to-top}

:::

## Connecting Outward {#connecting-outward}

Reaching systems and data beyond the conversation itself.

::: {.term-entry}
### MCP (Model Context Protocol)

An open standard for connecting Claude to external tools and data —
databases, issue trackers, internal systems — through "MCP servers," instead
of copy-pasting data in by hand. If a Skill is a recipe and an Agent is a
worker, MCP is the plug that lets either one reach outside systems safely.

**Want to know more?** [Official docs: MCP →](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp)
:::

:::
